name: Zamrock
about: Zamrock is the fuzz-heavy rock that came out of newly independent Zambia in the first half of the 1970s. President Kaunda's rule that radio play 95 per cent Zambian music, plus a copper boom and cheap Japanese amplifiers, produced a scene in Lusaka and the Copperbelt that absorbed Hendrix, Black Sabbath, James Brown and Osibisa and sang back in English, Bemba and Nyanja. WITCH, fronted by Emmanuel 'Jagari' Chanda, were the stars; Paul Ngozi's various bands were the heaviest; Amanaz and Rikki Ililonga's Musi-O-Tunya the most psychedelic. The copper crash, AIDS and vinyl's disappearance ended it by the early 1980s, and most of the musicians died young. Now-Again and Shadoks reissues since 2010 made the records collectible, and a reformed WITCH tours again.

artists.name: WITCH
artists.why: the scene's biggest and best band

artists.name: Salty Dog
artists.why: one of the scene's second-wave bands

artists.name: Blackfoot
artists.why: another of the scene's hard-rock bands

albums.title: Lazy Bones!!
albums.why: WITCH's fourth album, slowed to a stoned, bass-heavy crawl under Jagari's weary vocals; the Zamrock record most often cited as the genre's best.

albums.title: Africa
albums.why: Fuzz, melancholy and the slow burn of 'Khala My Friend'; the Shadoks reissue of this Lusaka one-off made it the genre's most loved record abroad.

albums.title: Introduction
albums.why: Generally held to be the first Zamrock LP, a set of garage rock and boogie that announced WITCH as the country's biggest band.

albums.title: 45,000 Volts
albums.why: Paul Ngozi's band at full distortion, the title a boast about the amplifiers; the heaviest and most Sabbath-like record the scene produced.

albums.title: My Ancestors
albums.why: Ngozi's drummer Chrissy Tembo stepping to the front for a raw, fuzz-caked set of acid rock and village memory; a Shadoks and Now-Again favourite.

albums.title: Wings of Africa
albums.why: Rikki Ililonga's band mixing Afro-rock horns and fuzz guitar on a loose, funky record that sits between Osibisa and the heavier Lusaka bands.

albums.title: Day of Judgement
albums.why: The Ngozi Family's first album, cruder than what followed but already fixed on moral warnings and Paul Ngozi's needling lead guitar.

albums.title: Zambia
albums.why: Ililonga's first solo record, gentler than Musi-O-Tunya, with acoustic songs and a politics of post-independence hope; a singer-songwriter inside Zamrock.

albums.title: Sunshine Love
albums.why: The follow-up adds funk and a bigger band to Ililonga's songs; warmer and more polished than his debut, if less distinctive.

albums.title: Black Power
albums.why: A Kitwe band's only album, with a title lifted from the American movement and a sound closer to Santana and Grand Funk; a Shadoks rescue.

albums.title: Dark Sunrise
albums.why: Now-Again's two-disc survey of Ililonga and Musi-O-Tunya's 1970s records, the clearest single document of the scene's most versatile musician.

albums.title: My Own Thing
albums.why: Now-Again's compilation of the guitarist's late-1970s recordings with Born Free, where Zamrock turns toward disco and reggae.

albums.title: Welcome to Zamrock! Vol. 1
albums.why: Egon's Now-Again anthology spreads the scene's fuzz and funk across two LPs with a book; the starting point for anyone outside Zambia.

albums.title: Welcome to Zamrock! Vol. 2
albums.why: The second volume digs deeper into the Zambia Music Parlour and Zambezi catalogues; as strong as the first, with more of the obscure bands.

note: Zamrock's original pressings are rare and poorly documented, so this list stops at the records whose credits and dates are certain; the Now-Again anthologies cover the rest.
